why.support: You can't stop a company getting hacked. But you can make your accounts hard to break into. And you can know what to do if it goes wrong.
why.core: You can't stop a company getting hacked. But you **can** make your own accounts hard to break into, spot the scams that follow, and know exactly what to do if something goes wrong.
why.extend: Your email, bank and socials hold your identity, your money and your name. Staying safe is mostly a few habits: long passphrases, two-step login, updates and a healthy suspicion. Plus a plan for when something goes wrong.

articles.title: Four habits that keep you safe

body.support:
Most accounts get hacked because of weak passwords or a bad click. Four habits stop most of it.

1. **Use a passphrase.** Four random words, like *purple-tractor-ocean-biscuit*. Long and easy to remember. Use a different one for each account.
2. **Turn on two-step login.** You type your password. Then a code from your phone. A stolen password alone won't work.
3. **Update** your phone and apps. Updates fix holes.
4. **Don't take the bait.** Fake messages say *Hurry! Click here!* Don't click. Open the real app yourself.

Protect your **email** first. It can reset all your other accounts.

If you're hacked: **change** the password, **turn on** two-step login, **check** what changed, and **report** it.
body.core:
Most accounts aren't hacked by genius hackers. They're broken into because of weak passwords, reused passwords, or a click on the wrong link. Four habits stop most of it.

1. **Use passphrases.** Four or more random words, like *purple-tractor-ocean-biscuit*. They're long, which makes them hard to crack, and easy to remember. Use a different one for each important account.
2. **Turn on two-step login.** After your password, you also enter a code from your phone or an app. A stolen password alone won't work.
3. **Update.** Phone and app updates fix security holes. Turn on automatic updates.
4. **Don't take the bait.** **Phishing** messages pretend to be your bank, a delivery company or a friend. They're urgent and they want you to click a link or share a code. Go to the app or website yourself instead.

Protect your **email** first. Whoever controls your email can reset almost every other account.

If you're hacked: **change** the password, **turn on** two-step login, **check** what's been changed or sent, and **report** it to the platform. Big cases can go to ReportCyber at cyber.gov.au.
body.extend:
Most account takeovers aren't clever. They use weak or reused passwords, old software, and people clicking in a hurry. Four habits shut most of those doors.

1. **Passphrases.** A string of four or more random words (*purple-tractor-ocean-biscuit*) is long enough to resist guessing and easy to remember. Use a unique one for every important account, or a password manager to keep track.
2. **Multi-factor authentication** (two-step login). A second check, like an app code, means a stolen password isn't enough.
3. **Updates.** Most updates fix security holes, so turning on automatic updates is cheap protection.
4. **Suspicion.** **Phishing** messages pretend to be brands or friends, rush you, and push you to a link or a code. Never act from the message itself. Go to the real app or site.

Protect your **email** first: it's the reset key for nearly everything else.

If an account is compromised: change the password, enable two-step login, review what's been changed or sent, and report it to the platform. Serious cases can be reported to ReportCyber (cyber.gov.au).

caseStudies.title: The Optus data breach

body.support:
In **September 2022**, a phone company called **Optus** was hacked. The details of millions of customers were stolen.

It was things like names, birthdays, phone numbers and emails. For some people, it was also their **address** and **licence number**.

The customers did nothing wrong. But they had to protect themselves. Some got new licences. They watched their bank accounts. And they looked out for **scam texts**.

The lesson: you can't stop a company being hacked. But you can lock down your own accounts.
body.core:
In **September 2022**, the phone company **Optus** said it had been hacked. The details of millions of customers, past and present, had been taken. Up to about **9.8 million** people were caught up.

For most, it was names, birthdays, phone numbers and emails. For some, it was also **home addresses** and **licence or passport numbers**.

The customers had done nothing wrong. But they still had to protect themselves. Some got new licences. They watched their bank accounts. And they looked out for **scam calls and texts** that used the news to trick them.

The lesson: you can't control what a company does with your data. You **can** lock down your own accounts, and be extra careful with messages after a breach.
body.extend:
In **September 2022**, the phone company **Optus** said it had been hit by a cyberattack. The personal details of up to about **9.8 million** current and former customers were taken.

For most people, the stolen data was names, birthdays, phone numbers and emails. For some, it also included **home addresses** and **licence or passport numbers**. Those are the details criminals need to steal an identity.

The customers had done nothing wrong, yet they had to do the clean-up. Many replaced their licences, and some states paid for this. People checked their bank accounts and dodged a wave of **scam calls and texts** that used the news.

The breach started a national debate about how much data companies should keep. For each of us, it showed that security is shared. Companies must protect our data, but our own habits limit the damage when they fail.

teacher.overview: Students learn the features and importance of digital security (passphrases, two-step login, updates, phishing) and safe practices online, read a phishing text closely, complete a private security check-up, and create a guide for younger students. The case study is the 2022 Optus data breach.
prep: Check your school's ICT policy on students changing account settings during class.
Optional: have the Australian Cyber Security Centre's “Protect yourself” pages open (cyber.gov.au).

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Why it matters
steps: **Hook (10 min):** the Optus breach headline. Who got a letter? (Many families did.)
**Explicit teaching (10 min):** the four habits; email as master key.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Spot it, check it
steps: **Annotate (15 min):** phishing SMS; share real scam texts students have received (no personal info).
**Check-up (20 min):** private security check-up on their own phones/accounts.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Teach it
steps: **Plan + make (25 min):** the guide for Year 7s (paper or Canva).
**Check & reflect (15 min):** quick check, reflection, request sign-off.

teacher.answers:
**Sort:** Fluffy2009 — weak; purple-tractor… — strong; same password everywhere — weak; two-step on email — strong; Password123! — weak; ignoring updates — weak.

**Phishing SMS:** 1 fake sender name; 2 urgency; 3 small payment to get card details; 4 lookalike link; 5 asks for a one-time code; 6 unexpected.

**Case study:** names, DOBs, phone numbers, emails; for some, addresses and licence/passport numbers. Customers replaced IDs, watched accounts and avoided scams; scammers exploit the news and the stolen details.

resources.label: Australian Cyber Security Centre — Protect yourself

realityCheck: **Privacy first.** The check-up must stay private: never ask students to show passwords, codes or settings. Say this out loud before they start.
**School devices and policies.** Students may not be allowed to change settings on school devices or be on their phones. Check your policy; the check-up can be done at home and discussed next lesson.
**Some students will have been hacked or scammed.** It can be embarrassing. Make it normal (“it happens to adults all the time”) and offer the hacked plan privately.
**Most engaging part:** students sharing real scam texts they've had. You'll get plenty. Keep personal details out.
**Works in a real class:** yes. It's highly relevant and the outcome is a real behaviour change. Give it all three lessons; the check-up and guide are where the learning sticks.
